etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hummen (“to hum, buzz, drone, make a murmuring sound to cover embarrassment”); akin to Dutch hommelen (“to bumble, buzz”), dialectal Dutch hommen (“to buzz, hum”), Middle High German hummen (“to hum”), probably ultimately of imitative origin.

definitions.definition: A hummed tune, i.e. created orally with lips closed.
An often indistinct sound resembling human humming.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: the shard-borne beetle with his drowsy hums

definitions.definition: Busy activity, like the buzz of a beehive.

quote.citation: c. 1622, John Fletcher, Philip Massinger [et al.?], “Beggars Bush”, in Comedies and Tragedies […], London:  […]  Humphrey Robinson, […], and for Humphrey Moseley […], published 1647, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: you do provide me hum enough , And lour to bouse with

definitions.definition: (with article) A phenomenon, or collection of phenomena, involving widespread reports of a persistent and invasive low-frequency humming, rumbling, or droning noise not audible to all people.

quote.citation: 2011 June 13, “Who, What, Why: Why is 'the hum' such a mystery?”, in BBC News‎[1]:
quote.text: There is a range of theories from farm or factory machinery to conspiracy theories such as flying saucers. And yet, "the hum" remains an unsolved case.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To make a sound from the vocal cords without pronouncing any real words, with one's lips closed.
(intransitive) To drone like certain insects naturally do in motion, or sounding similarly.

quote.citation: 1769, Firishta, translated by Alexander Dow, Tales translated from the Persian of Inatulla of Delhi, volume I, Dublin: P. and W. Wilson et al., page iv:
quote.text: The leaves of the foreſt were loaded with manna, pure amber dropped from every bough, honey diſtilled from the rifted rock, and the humming bee, drunk with joy, ſtrayed from flower to flower, forgetful of his burſting cells.

quote.citation: 1922 October 26, Virginia Woolf, chapter 2, in Jacob’s Room, Richmond, London:  […]  Leonard & Virginia Woolf at the Hogarth Press, →OCLC; republished London: The Hogarth Press, 1960, →OCLC:
quote.text: A slight gloom fell upon the table. Jacob was helping himself to jam; the postman was talking to Rebecca in the kitchen; there was a bee humming at the yellow flower which nodded at the open window.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To buzz, be busily active like a beehive
(intransitive) To produce low sounds which blend continuously
(transitive, UK, dated, slang) To flatter by approving; to cajole; to deceive or impose upon; to humbug.
Synonym of hmm: a noise indicating thought, consideration, &c.

quote.citation: 1890 February, A[rthur] Conan Doyle, “The Baker Street Irregulars”, in The Sign of Four (Standard Library), London: Spencer Blackett […], →OCLC, page 157:

definitions.definition: Synonym of um: a noise indicating doubt, uncertainty, &c.

quote.citation: 1991 September, Stephen Fry, chapter 1, in The Liar, London: Heinemann, →ISBN, →OCLC, section I, page 19:
quote.text: Ah, now this is why we must proceed with great circumspection. They were both, hum, “put out” themselves.
